narrative: The model estimated a 41% chance that you would be a bad credit risk. That means that, in similar cases, about 41 out of 100 would be expected to run into repayment problems; it is below an even chance, but it was above the bank’s approval threshold, so the application was denied. The strongest factor behind the decision was your checking-account status. Being below zero DM was the most influential reason pushing toward bad credit; among approved applicants, this is much less common than having no balance problems, at 12.6% versus 59.2%. The second most important factor was your repayment burden: an installment rate of 2% of disposable income, below the approved average of about 3%, pushed toward good credit. The third was the requested term: 12 months, shorter than the approved average of about 19 months, also pushed toward good credit. Thus, two favorable factors helped you, but they did not outweigh the checking-account concern. To improve your next application, bring the checking account into positive standing and avoid overdrafts for a sustained period, keep other credit obligations low, and ask the lender what account history or balance evidence would meet its criteria before reapplying. Your sex, age and foreign-worker status were not used.
